title: Powdered Sugar vs Granulated Sugar: Why a Cup-for-Cup Swap Can Fail

seo.title: Powdered vs Granulated Sugar: Not 1:1
seo.meta_description: Powdered sugar is finely milled and usually contains a little starch to prevent caking. A cup weighs roughly 120 g versus about 200 g for granulated sugar, so volume-for-volume swaps change sweetness and structure.
seo.search_intent: Explain why powdered and granulated sugar differ by volume and how that affects baking substitutions.

excerpt: Powdered and granulated sugar are both mostly sucrose, but a cup of powdered sugar contains much less mass—about 120 g versus roughly 200 g for granulated. Powdered sugar also usually contains starch, so it is not a simple cup-for-cup replacement.
content_html:
Powdered sugar and granulated sugar can start from the same sucrose, yet they fill a measuring cup very differently. Powdered sugar is milled into tiny particles that trap air, and commercial versions usually contain a little starch to resist clumping.

A cup does not contain the same mass

A useful baking reference is about 200 grams for 1 cup granulated sugar and roughly 120 grams for 1 cup unsifted powdered sugar. Packing and brand can shift those numbers, but not enough to erase the gap.

About 1 cupWeightPractical effect
Granulated sugar≈200 gMore sucrose per cup
Powdered sugar≈120 gLess mass per cup, often with added starch

Replacing 1 cup granulated with 1 cup powdered can therefore cut the sugar mass by around 40%, changing sweetness, spread, browning, and moisture management.

Starch is part of the package

U.S. confectioners' sugar commonly includes cornstarch to keep the powder free-flowing. That is helpful in frosting and glaze, but the starch can slightly thicken or dry a delicate mixture.

Particle size changes the job

Powdered sugar dissolves almost immediately, which makes it ideal for icing and buttercream. Granulated sugar provides crystals that help aerate butter during creaming and influence how cookies spread and crisp.

Weight is safer than volume—but not always identical

If a substitution is structurally reasonable, matching sugar by weight is much closer than matching by cups. Even then, the starch and particle size can alter the finished texture.

For baking, treat powdered and granulated sugar as different functional ingredients, not two measuring-cup versions of the same thing.

faq.question: Does 1 cup powdered sugar equal 1 cup granulated sugar?
faq.answer: No. A cup of granulated sugar is about 200 g, while a cup of powdered sugar is roughly 120 g, so a cup-for-cup swap changes the actual sugar mass dramatically.

faq.question: Why does powdered sugar contain cornstarch?
faq.answer: A small amount of starch helps absorb moisture and prevents the fine sugar particles from caking.

faq.question: Can I make powdered sugar at home?
faq.answer: A high-powered blender can make a fine sugar powder, though commercial confectioners' sugar is usually more uniform and often contains starch.
